title: A Stolen Blessing Splits a Family
overview: Jacob and his mother trick the blind, aging Isaac into giving Jacob the family blessing meant for Esau, and the fallout tears the family apart.

parts.label: Isaac plans to bless Esau (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: A father's final blessing was seen as a binding word that passed on leadership of the family and God's promises, often sealed with a shared meal. Before the twins were born, Rebekah had been told the older would serve the younger (25:23), and the story leaves open how much Isaac knew or weighed that.

parts.label: Rebekah's scheme (vv. 5-17)
parts.note: Rebekah cooks goat meat to taste like wild game, then disguises Jacob with Esau's best clothes and goatskins over his smooth skin. Jacob objects only that he might get caught and cursed, not that the plan is wrong.

parts.label: Jacob deceives his father (vv. 18-29)
parts.note: Jacob lies outright, even crediting God for his quick hunt, and Isaac, unsure about the voice, is won over by touch and smell. Dew, rich soil, grain and wine meant prosperity in a dry land, and the promise of rule over nations and brothers was later read as pointing to Israel, Jacob's descendants.

parts.label: Esau discovers the trick (vv. 30-38)
parts.note: Isaac trembles but says the blessing stands, reflecting the belief that a solemn spoken blessing could not be taken back. In v. 36 Esau puns on Jacob's name, which sounds like the Hebrew for "heel" and can suggest "he cheats," and he recalls the birthright Jacob got for a bowl of stew (25:29-34).

parts.label: Esau's lesser blessing (vv. 39-40)
parts.note: The Hebrew can mean Esau's home will be either "of" or "away from" the earth's richness, so translations differ, though most modern ones read it as a harder life. It looks ahead to Edom, the people descended from Esau, who were later ruled by Israel and then broke free (2 Kings 8:20).

parts.label: Esau's rage, Jacob's escape (vv. 41-46)
parts.note: Esau plans to kill Jacob once their father dies, so Rebekah sends Jacob to her brother Laban in Harran, afraid of losing both sons at once. She gets Isaac's agreement by raising the problem of Esau's Hittite wives, who had already caused them grief (26:34-35).

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the story quietly sides with Rebekah and Jacob as carrying out God's stated plan by wrong means, or shows every member of the family at fault and God's purpose going forward in spite of them all.
think: Can a good outcome ever make up for the dishonest way it was reached?
